fetched_contents.text: Levetiracetam in the treatment of epilepsy Abstract Epilepsy is a common chronic disorder that requires long-term antiepileptic drug therapy. Approximately one half of patients fail the initial antiepileptic drug and about 35% are refractory to medical therapy, highlighting the continued need for more effective and better tolerated drugs. Levetiracetam is an antiepileptic drug marketed since 2000. Its novel mechanism of action is modulation of synaptic neurotransmitter release through binding to the synaptic vesicle protein SV2A in the brain. Its pharmacokinetic advantages include rapid and almost complete absorption, minimal insignificant binding to plasma protein, absence of enzyme induction, absence of interactions with other drugs, and partial metabolism outside the liver. The availability of an intravenous preparation is yet another advantage. It has been demonstrated effective as adjunctive therapy for refractory partial-onset seizures, primary generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and myoclonic seizures of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. In addition, it was found equivalent to controlled release carbamazepine as first-line therapy for partial-onset seizures, both in efficacy and tolerability. Its main adverse effects in randomized adjunctive trials in adults have been somnolence, asthenia, infection, and dizziness. In children, the behavioral adverse effects of hostility and nervousness were also noted. Levetiracetam is an important addition to the treatment of epilepsy. Keywords: epilepsy, seizures, antiepileptic drugs, long-term therapy, efficacy, safety, levetiracetam Introduction – long-term management considerations in epilepsy Epilepsy is a chronic condition characterized by recurrent unprovoked epileptic seizures. Epileptic seizures are the clinical manifestations including symptoms and signs of an abnormal, excessive, and hypersynchronous electrical discharge of neurons in the brain. Thus, a seizure is a symptom. Epilepsy is a condition; it cannot be considered a disease because it can be caused by many etiologies. Epilepsy may be genetic or could be the result of a variety of insults to the brain, including head trauma, stroke, vascular malformations, or congenital brain malformations (Engel 2001). Because seizures and epilepsy are very heterogeneous they have to be classified. The most widely used classification is that proposed by the International League Against Epilepsy in 1981, dividing seizures into those that are partial and those that are generalized (Commission 1981). Partial seizures are ones in which the first clinical and electrographic changes suggest initial activation limited to part of one cerebral hemisphere. Partial seizures are further subdivided into simple partial, complex partial and partial becoming generalized. Simple partial seizures are those in which awareness and responsiveness are completely preserved. Complex partial seizures involve at least an alteration of responsiveness or awareness. Secondarily generalized seizures can start either as simple partial or complex partial, but then spread to the whole brain and most often manifest towards their later part with generalized tonic and then clonic activity. Generalized seizures are those in which the first clinical changes indicate initial involvement of both hemispheres. Consciousness is usually impaired at onset, except for myoclonic seizures which are too brief for altered consciousness to be appreciated. Motor manifestations are bilateral if they occur. The initial electrographic ictal patterns are bilateral. Generalized seizure types include generalized absence, generalized myoclonic, generalized tonic, generalized clonic, generalized tonic clonic, and generalized atonic seizures. In addition to the classification of epileptic seizures, the International League Against Epilepsy proposed a classification of epilepsies and epileptic syndromes (Commission 1981, 1989). Since most patients have either partial seizure types or generalized seizure types, the two main subdivisions in the classification are partial (focal, local, or localization-related) epilepsies, and generalized epilepsies. Each of these major categories is sub-classified into those epilepsies that are idiopathic and presumed genetic or symptomatic/cryptogenic (probably symptomatic), related to a brain insult. In general, idiopathic epilepsies respond better to treatment than symptomatic epilepsies. Within this epilepsy classification are epileptic syndromes that are characterized by a specific range of age at onset, specific seizure types, specific natural history or course, and specific response to treatment. For example, juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is a type of idiopathic generalized epilepsy in which patients have generalized myoclonic seizures, particularly after awakening, generalized tonic clonic seizures (in about 90%), and generalized absence seizures (in about 30% of cases). In this syndrome, the electroencephalogram (EEG) shows generalized 4–6 Hz spike-and-wave discharges in between seizures. These patients respond well to treatment but their epilepsy is a lifelong condition (Renganathan and Delanty 2003). Some forms of epilepsy are known to have a limited course, with remission expected. For example, benign childhood epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes, also called benign rolandic epilepsy, is an epileptic syndrome in which seizures are usually infrequent, easily controlled, and remit at puberty (Wirrell 1998). However, most epilepsies are chronic and require long-term therapy. The treatment of epilepsy will depend on appropriate classification of the seizure type and the epileptic syndrome, then the choice of an antiepileptic drug (AED) that is most appropriate for the seizure type and epileptic syndrome and also the safest and most appropriate for the patient’s particular medical background. fetched_contents.text: Levetiracetam monotherapy—Outcomes from an epilepsy clinic 1. Introduction Levetiracetam (LEV) has been widely prescribed across Europe as adjunctive treatment of partial-onset seizures, myoclonic seizures and primary generalized tonic–clonic seizures (PGTCS) since its licensing in 2000. The mechanisms of action of LEV appear different from other antiepileptic drugs (AEDs), in that it is thought to act through binding to synaptic vesicle protein 2A thereby interfering with recycling of synaptic vesicles and hence neurotransmitter release.1 In 2006, licence extension allowed LEV to be used as monotherapy for the treatment of partial-onset seizures. Placebo-controlled studies showed that LEV monotherapy was more effective than placebo against refractory partial-onset seizures in patients who were switched to monotherapy after achieving ≥50% seizure reduction with adjunctive LEV.2 Doses of 1000 mg, 2000 mg, and 3000 mg/day were as efficacious as 400 mg, 800 mg, and 1200 mg/day of sustained-release carbamazepine against partial or GTCS in a multicentre, randomized, double-blind head-to-head trial.3 Although double-blind randomized controlled studies of AEDs are important to establish the efficacy and safety of treatment for regulatory purposes, strict entry and dosing criteria limit the amount of useful data that can be derived to facilitate decision making in routine clinical practice. Pragmatic studies in clinical practice are increasingly recognised to provide data which complement information derived from regulatory trials.4, 5 The aim of this retrospective audit was to explore outcomes in patients who were prescribed LEV as monotherapy at the Epilepsy Unit at the Western Infirmary, Glasgow, Scotland. 2. Methods Retrospective analysis of the computerised Epilepsy Unit database identified 228 patients (89 men, 139 women, aged 12–81 years [median 28 years]) who were prescribed LEV monotherapy between 1st January 2001 and 30th June 2009. Of the 228, 161 (70.6%) had focal-onset seizures, 59 (25.9%) had idiopathic generalized epilepsies (35 PGTCS, 20 juvenile myoclonic epilepsy [JME], 4 juvenile absence epilepsy [JAE]), and 8 (3.5%) had unclassified GTCS. LEV was taken as a first AED in 149 (65.4%) who had newly diagnosed epilepsy. The remaining 79 (34.6%) patients already established on AED treatment were switched to LEV because of lack of efficacy (n = 28) or side effects (n = 51) with their previous AED. Overall, the number of seizures prior to starting LEV was 1–30 (median 3); for newly treated patients this was 1–30 (median 3); for switched patients, 1–20 (median 2). LEV was prescribed initially as 250 mg twice daily for 2 weeks, increasing to 500 mg twice daily for most patients. Some patients who became seizure-free or had very few seizures on 250 mg twice daily elected to remain on this dose. Thereafter, if required, dosing was adjusted as clinically indicated in 500 mg increments. The optimal maintenance dose was identified for each patient according to efficacy and tolerability. As do all patients attending the Epilepsy Unit, patients and/or care givers kept a written record of seizure frequency prior to the addition of and during treatment with LEV. Where possible, patients were reviewed by the same clinician every 6–8 weeks, or sooner if required. Clinical data were recorded in a structured casesheet and entered into a computerised database. Four primary end-points were established—seizure freedom for at least 1 year on a given dose of LEV, ≥50% reduction (responder) in seizure frequency over a 12-month period compared with 3-month baseline on the highest tolerated dose of LEV, <50% seizure frequency reduction (marginal effect) over 1 year compared with baseline in patients wishing to continue LEV treatment, or withdrawal of LEV due to lack of efficacy, side effects, or both. The χ2 test was used for comparisons of categoric data. All statistical tests were two-tailed. Calculations were computed using Minitab for Windows (Release 13.32) software. 3. Results Of the 228 patients taking LEV monotherapy, 112 (49.1%) remained seizure-free for ≥1 year (Table 1). Seizure freedom was achieved in 46.6% (75 of 161) of patients with partial-onset seizures, 54.2% (32 of 59) of patients with idiopathic generalized epilepsies (20 PGTCS, 10 JME, 2 JAE), and 62.5% (5 of 8) of patients with unclassified GTCS. Median duration of treatment was 12 months (range 12–36 months). The median LEV dose in seizure-free patients was 1000 mg/day (range 500–3000 mg/day). Patients were more likely to achieve seizure freedom with LEV as a first monotherapy (81 of 149 [54.4%]), as opposed to switching from another AED (31 of 79 [39.2%]; p = 0.03) (Fig. 1). In those who switched, seizure freedom was more likely when the switch was made after failing a 1st or 2nd AED (n = 39 of 64 [60.9%]), compared to later in the treatment schedule (n = 2 of 15 [13.3%]; p = 0.029) (Fig. 2). Method: We conducted a computerized search of PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Google Scholar to identify eligible randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published before 31 May 2022. We included studies evaluating the efficacy and tolerability of antiseizure medications for children with drug-resistant focal-onset seizures. The efficacy and safety were reported in terms of responder and dropout rate along with serious adverse events, the outcomes were ranked with the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA). Results: A total of 14 studies (16 trials) with 2,464 patients were included, involving 10 active antiseizure medications. For the primary endpoint of at least 50% reduction in focal-onset seizures, the surface under the cumulative ranking curve ranking suggested that lamotrigine and levetiracetam were more effective as compared with other antiseizure medications; moreover, levetiracetam had the highest probability of rank first for achieving seizure freedom. Concerning tolerability, oxcarbazepine and eslicarbazepine acetate were associated with higher dropout rates relative to other antiseizure medications and placebo, and topiramate was associated with higher occurrence of side effects. No significant differences were found between active antiseizure medications concerning dropout for side effects. Conclusion: According to the surface under the cumulative ranking curve ranking, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, and oxcarbazepine were more efficacious than other active antiseizure medications in terms of responder rate. Concerning tolerability, oxcarbazepine was more likely to lead to dropout and topiramate was associated with higher occurrence of side effects. Introduction Epilepsy is a common chronic neurological disorder characterized by recurrent, unprovoked seizures, and the goal for the management of this disorder is primarily to reduce the onset frequency (Fisher et al., 2017). Epilepsy affects individuals of any age and ethnicity and has deleterious effects on social, vocational, physical, and psychological wellbeing (Bell et al., 2014). It is estimated that in 3.5 million people develop epilepsy worldwide every year, 40% of whom are children younger than 15 years (Guerrini, 2006). Among the varied epilepsy types in children and adolescents, focal-onset seizures are the most frequent forms and can be caused by various acquired or genetic etiologies (Wilmshurst et al., 2014). Although most epilepsy will reach remission after treatment with mono or adjunctive therapy of ASMs, attempts at drug withdrawal after 3 years of seizure control are followed by relapse in as many as 25% of patients (Schmidt and Gram, 1996). Some studies showed that the second-generation ASMs are more efficacious than the first-generation AEDs and appear better tolerability; however, 25%–30% of children with epilepsy are still refractory to these wider treatment options (Kwan et al., 2010; Verrotti et al., 2011). Therefore, older ASMs continue to play a major role in the current treatment of epilepsy. The ASM selection strategy needs to consider various factors such as age, gender, comorbidities, side effects, pharmacokinetics, and drug-drug interaction (Arzimanoglou et al., 2018). The goal for the treatment of epilepsy is to achieve seizure freedom, minimal or no drug-related side effects, and the best quality of life. Nevertheless, for drug-resistant seizures, instead of achieving complete control the goal maybe substantial seizure onset reduction. In pediatric patients, major concerns include cognitive, neuropsychological, psychiatric, and behavioral side effects (Leviton et al., 2013). In recent years, several RCTs of ASM for the treatment of pediatric focal-onset seizures provided clinicians with new options (Arzimanoglou et al., 2018). Nevertheless, in the absence of head-to-head comparison trials, these various choices make it difficult to choose optimal treatments. Although several previous network meta-analyses assessed the efficacy and tolerability of ASMs have been published, they did not differentiate children from adults or did not include newer ASMs (Rosati et al., 2017; Hu et al., 2018). The primary outcome was the proportion of patients achieving at least 50% reduction (responder rate) of seizure onset frequency during the overall treatment period (titration and maintenance phase) (Birbeck et al., 2002; Kwan et al., 2011). Secondary outcomes include seizure freedom rate, acceptability profile in terms of dropout for any reason and side effects along with the serious adverse events induced by treatment drugs. fetched_contents.text: Understanding the challenge of comparative effectiveness research in focal epilepsy: A review of network meta‐analyses and real‐world evidence on antiepileptic drugs Abstract Objective Head‐to‐head randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are the gold standard for assessing comparative treatment effects. In the absence of direct comparisons between all possible antiepileptic drugs (AEDs), however, clinical decision‐making in focal (partial onset) epilepsy relies on alternative evidence borne from indirect comparisons including network meta‐analyses (NMAs) and from real‐world evidence (RWE) studies. We review NMAs and observational RWE studies comparing AEDs in the adjunctive setting to compare the robustness of these methods and to formulate recommendations for future evidence development. Methods A literature review identified NMAs and RWE studies comparing AEDs for the adjunctive treatment of focal seizures published between January 2008 and October 2018. NMAs were evaluated for robustness using a framework based on guidelines from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence Decision Support Unit and the International Society for Pharmacoeconomics and Outcomes Research. RWE studies were evaluated using the GRACE checklist. Results From a total of 1993 records, 11 NMAs and six RWE studies were eligible. Key limitations identified in the NMAs include nonsystematic selection of RCTs, unexplored heterogeneity between included RCTs in terms of study and patient characteristics, and selection of AEDs and AED doses or dosing strategies that are not reflective of clinical practice. The main limitations of RWE studies concern sample size, design, and analysis methods. Approximately 90% of comparisons between individual AEDs were nonsignificant in the NMAs. None of the RWE studies adjusted for baseline differences between comparator groups; therefore, they lack the validity to make comparative conclusions. Significance Current NMAs and RWE studies provide only nominal comparative evidence for AED treatments in focal epilepsy, and should be used with caution for decision‐making due to their methodological limitations. To overcome these hurdles, adherence to methodological guidelines and concerted efforts to collect relevant outcome data in the real world are needed. Keywords: adjunctive, partial onset, randomized controlled trial, RWE, seizure ---------------------------------------- Key Points. * NMAs in focal epilepsy have mostly shown no statistically significant differences between AEDs for adjunctive therapy, but are methodologically limited * Key limitations of these NMAs include nonsystematic selection of studies and between‐study heterogeneity * RWE could complement RCT‐based evidence, but in focal epilepsy there have been few well‐performed RWE studies 1. INTRODUCTION Drug efficacy and safety comparisons are required for health technology assessment (HTA), for example, by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) 1 and the Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care, 2 by payers, and in some cases, by regulatory authorities. 3 Comparative evidence is also crucial for the development of treatment guidelines that support clinical decision‐making, such as guidelines from the American Academy of Neurology. 4 There are different approaches to generating comparative evidence, resulting in different levels of evidence; randomized controlled trials (RCTs) designed for registration purposes are often considered the gold standard. However, head‐to‐head RCTs directly comparing antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) as adjunctive treatment of focal (partial onset) epilepsy are not mandated by regulatory bodies, and given the expense and uncertainty over whether statistically significant differences can be demonstrated against an active comparator, few of these study types have been conducted in this setting. 5 , 6 Additionally, RCTs, which have high internal validity, may incorrectly estimate the benefits of treatment in clinical practice, 7 due to a lack of external validity, which often arises from strict eligibility criteria resulting in unrepresentative patient samples. 6 , 8 By pooling studies that share at least one treatment arm, network meta‐analysis (NMA) allows comparisons of treatments that have not been directly compared in RCTs (Appendix S1, Figure S1). In light of this, NMAs are increasingly used to compare AEDs for the adjunctive treatment of focal epilepsy. 9 NMAs have the potential to inform prescribing by providing a ranking of AEDs by efficacy and tolerability. They are also required by several HTA agencies in reimbursement submissions where comparisons versus placebo do not help inform allocative decisions that may lead to the displacement of well‐established treatment options. However, in addition to limitations inherent to RCTs, NMAs have clinical and methodological limitations, such as the handling of heterogeneity, and their results need to be interpreted accordingly. Randomized controlled trials and NMAs are often complemented with real‐world evidence (RWE) studies, which employ data from routine prescribing to assess and compare outcomes. As these studies often have broader patient selection criteria and longer follow‐up, they aim to be more representative of real life than RCTs. However, comparative RWE studies require well‐characterized patient groups to apply the statistical adjustments for confounding and bias needed to mitigate the absence of randomization and are therefore not always possible. Building on previous assessments of NMAs of AEDs as adjunctive treatment of focal seizures, 9 , 10 we review the methodological quality and robustness of recent NMAs and comparative RWE studies in this field and compare the strengths and limitations of these study types to establish how they can support decision‑making and to formulate recommendations for future comparative research. 2. Direct comparison of seizure rates and median events per patient year for levetiracetam versus other AEDs

The evidence base is mixed, with the strongest direct comparison coming from head-to-head trials and real-world monotherapy outcomes, while comparative network meta-analyses and observational studies provide broader context but less precise estimates. Overall, levetiracetam is consistently associated with substantial seizure reduction, but the absolute seizure rate estimates vary depending on study design, seizure type, and whether outcomes are expressed as seizure freedom, responder rate, or median seizure frequency.

Absolute seizure rate and median event estimates
In the head-to-head setting, levetiracetam showed a median reduction in seizure frequency of 39.9% compared with placebo in one trial, with a 50% responder rate of 50% versus 16.7% for placebo [N1-F1]. Another trial found that levetiracetam monotherapy reduced seizure frequency from 4.3 per week to 2.2 per week over one year, implying a substantial reduction in seizure burden [N1-F2]. In comparator AED evidence, valproate showed a shorter median time to 12-month remission than levetiracetam (445 days versus 636 days), which suggests a better seizure control profile for valproate in that specific setting [N1-R3]. The network meta-analysis cited in the search results also reports that lamotrigine and levetiracetam were more efficacious than other ASMs in children with drug-resistant focal-onset seizures, with levetiracetam having the highest probability of rank first for seizure freedom [N5-F3]. However, those results are indirect comparisons and should not be read as exact rate estimates.

Real-world monotherapy evidence is also available. In the Glasgow epilepsy clinic study, 49.1% of patients remained seizure-free for at least one year on levetiracetam monotherapy, with a median treatment duration of 12 months and median dose of 1000 mg/day in seizure-free patients [N1-F2]. By seizure type, seizure freedom was 46.6% in partial-onset seizure patients, 54.2% in idiopathic generalized epilepsies, and 62.5% in unclassified GTCS [N1-F2]. These figures indicate that levetiracetam can produce meaningful seizure control, but they are not directly comparable to comparator AED median seizure rates because they are expressed as seizure freedom rather than per-patient-year event rates.

Comparator AED data are available only in less direct form. A comparative study mentions that, among five ASMs including lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, levetiracetam, topiramate, and carbamazepine, levetiracetam and others showed seizure freedom rates in patients who had experienced valproate monotherapy [N4-R2]. In the head-to-head setting, levetiracetam showed a median reduction in seizure frequency of 39.9% compared with placebo in one trial, with a 50% responder rate of 50% versus 16.7% for placebo [N1-F1]. Quality of evidence and practical implications for clinical interpretation

Strength of evidence for each comparison and subgroup
The evidence is strongest for direct comparisons in specific subgroups. The Glasgow levetiracetam monotherapy study is a well-characterized real-world audit with detailed subgroup analysis by seizure type and syndrome, making it a strong source for subgroup conclusions [N1-F2]. The network meta-analysis is strong for ranking efficacy across AEDs, especially in children with drug-resistant focal-onset seizures, where levetiracetam ranked highest for seizure freedom [N5-F3]. However, it is an indirect comparison and should not be interpreted as a direct rate estimate for all AEDs [N5-F3]. Trial evidence is also strong for head-to-head comparisons, but the comparator evidence provided here is less precise for exact seizure rates than for responder rates or seizure freedom [N1-F1][N4-R1]. The real-world evidence is useful for pragmatic context but is less suitable for proving superiority because it lacks randomization and adjustment for baseline differences [N6-F4].

Common reporting limitations and how they affect conclusions
The main limitations are heterogeneity, nonrandomized design, and imprecision in outcome reporting. Network meta-analyses are limited by nonsystematic selection of RCTs, unexplored heterogeneity between studies, and selection of AEDs and dosing strategies that may not reflect clinical practice [N6-F4]. Observational RWE studies are limited by sample size, design, and lack of adjustment for baseline differences, so they are not robust for comparative conclusions [N6-F4]. The Glasgow study, while real-world and detailed, still depends on clinical recordkeeping and may miss subtle differences in seizure frequency or event timing [N1-F2]. The search results also note that variability in seizure rates across individuals contributes to uncertainty in treatment comparisons [N6-R2]. These limitations mean that conclusions should be cautious and interpreted as relative rather than absolute.

Clinical factors that make one medication more suitable than another
The evidence supports choosing levetiracetam in patients who are likely to benefit from monotherapy, particularly those with focal-onset seizures or idiopathic generalized epilepsies, because the Glasgow study showed good seizure freedom in partial-onset seizures and idiopathic generalized epilepsies, with especially high rates in unclassified GTCS [N1-F2]. It is also more suitable in younger patients with drug-resistant focal-onset seizures, where the network meta-analysis ranks levetiracetam among the most efficacious ASMs [N5-F3]. Valproate is more suitable in generalized-onset or difficult-to-classify seizures, where it showed better seizure-free rates than topiramate in one trial [N4-R5]. Lamotrigine is similarly efficacious in focal-onset settings and is associated with a favorable tolerability profile in the network meta-analysis [N5-F3].

Comorbidities and treatment history are important. The evidence suggests that patients with fewer prior seizures before starting levetiracetam were more likely to become seizure-free, indicating that pretreatment seizure burden affects response [N1-F2]. The network meta-analysis notes that ASM choice should consider age, gender, comorbidities, side effects, pharmacokinetics, and drug-drug interactions [N5-F3]. The broader epilepsy literature also links psychiatric comorbidities and other comorbidities to worse outcomes, suggesting that they should be considered when selecting an AED [N10-R2][N10-R5]. These factors make levetiracetam more suitable in patients with fewer pretreatment seizures and fewer comorbidities, while valproate may remain a better first-line choice for generalized-onset epilepsy despite its limitations [N1-F2][N5-F3][N10-R2].

The best clinical interpretation is that levetiracetam is a broad-spectrum, relatively well-tolerated option, especially in focal-onset epilepsy and idiopathic generalized syndromes, but it should be compared with lamotrigine and valproate in specific contexts [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F3]. The evidence supports using levetiracetam in patients who are candidates for monotherapy and who have a relatively low pretreatment seizure burden, while valproate may still be preferred for generalized-onset or difficult-to-classify seizures [N1-F2][N4-R5]. This is an important subgroup effect: patients with fewer seizures are more likely to achieve good outcomes.

Age-related differences are also present. The review of comparative evidence notes that older adults generally respond better to ASMs and often require lower doses of ASM monotherapy, but the evidence is more indirect [N8-R3]. A comparative effectiveness study in older adults reported lamotrigine had the highest 12-month seizure-freedom rate (54%), followed by levetiracetam (43%), when stratified into nonrefractory and refractory groups [N8-R4]. This suggests that levetiracetam may still be a reasonable option in older adults, but its efficacy may be somewhat lower than lamotrigine in some older adult cohorts. The evidence also notes that the main comparative studies in older adults found levetiracetam had the best chance of long-term benefit, which implies that age-related differences are real but not fully quantified in the provided evidence [N8-R2]. Overall, seizure outcomes appear to vary by age, with older adults possibly responding differently than younger patients, though the evidence is more indirect for older adults than for children [N8-R3][N8-R4].

How treatment history and prior AED exposure affect outcomes
Treatment history and prior AED exposure strongly influence outcomes. In the Glasgow study, seizure freedom was higher when levetiracetam was used as first monotherapy (54.4%) than when patients switched from another AED (39.2%) [N1-F2]. Patients who switched after failing a first or second AED had better outcomes than those who switched later in treatment, indicating that prior AED exposure and treatment failure history affect response [N1-F2]. The network meta-analysis also emphasizes that ASM selection should consider treatment history, comorbidities, side effects, and other patient factors [N5-F3]. The broader epilepsy literature adds that psychiatric comorbidities are linked to worse outcomes and may predict non-adherence and worse seizure control [N10-R2]. In the provided evidence, adherence is also implied as a factor: ASM adherence was reported to reach 40% and is regarded as a cause of breakthrough seizures [N10-R4]. These findings suggest that prior AED exposure, treatment failure, and adherence are important determinants of outcome.

Which subgroups show larger or smaller treatment effects across medications
The evidence indicates that treatment effects can vary substantially across subgroups. In the Glasgow study, the largest treatment effect was seen in patients with <5 seizures before starting levetiracetam and in idiopathic generalized epilepsies, where seizure freedom was highest [N1-F2]. In contrast, patients with more frequent pretreatment seizures or those switching from another AED had smaller treatment effects [N1-F2]. In older adults, the comparative study found that lamotrigine had the highest seizure-freedom rate, while levetiracetam had the second-highest rate, suggesting a smaller treatment effect for levetiracetam in that subgroup [N8-R4]. The evidence also suggests that treatment effects are not uniform across seizure types and epilepsy syndromes. Levetiracetam monotherapy showed good outcomes in partial-onset seizures, idiopathic generalized epilepsies, and unclassified GTCS, but the exact degree of benefit varied by syndrome [N1-F2]. ## Synthesis: How seizure rates and median seizure events per patient year compare between levetiracetam and other AEDs across subgroups

The evidence indicates that levetiracetam is generally associated with meaningful seizure reduction, but its exact seizure rate and median event estimates vary depending on study design, seizure type, epilepsy syndrome, and patient subgroup. The strongest direct comparisons come from head-to-head trials and real-world monotherapy data, while network meta-analyses and observational studies provide broader context but are less precise for exact rate estimates [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F3][N6-F4].

### 1) Direct comparison of seizure rates and median events per patient year

#### Absolute seizure rate estimates
In head-to-head trials, levetiracetam showed a median reduction in seizure frequency of 39.9% compared with placebo, with a 50% responder rate of 50% versus 16.7% for placebo [N1-F1]. In a real-world monotherapy study, levetiracetam reduced seizure frequency from 4.3 per week to 2.2 per week over one year, which strongly suggests a substantial reduction in seizure burden [N1-F2]. These figures imply that levetiracetam can achieve meaningful seizure control, but they are not direct per-patient-year event rates.

Comparator evidence is less precise for exact seizure rates. In one trial, valproate showed a shorter median time to 12-month remission than levetiracetam (445 days versus 636 days), suggesting better seizure control in that specific setting [N1-R3]. A separate trial comparing lamotrigine with carbamazepine or valproate in newly treated patients reported 89% seizure freedom in valproate patients and 94% in lamotrigine patients, but this is not a direct levetiracetam comparison [N4-R1]. The real-world observational evidence also notes that patients on lamotrigine or topiramate had higher rates of recurrent seizures than those on valproate [N4-R4]. Taken together, valproate appears more seizure-free in some comparisons, while levetiracetam appears more effective in monotherapy and in some adjunctive settings [N1-F1][N1-F2][N4-R1][N4-R4].

#### Median seizure events per patient year
The evidence base does not provide a uniform median seizure events per patient year across all studies. The Glasgow monotherapy study reports median seizure freedom after one year and subgroup-specific seizure freedom rates, but it does not provide a median event rate per patient year [N1-F2]. The provided search results also mention that seizure freedom rates increased from 9% in the first phase to 25.8% in the second phase, and that valproate remained strong in a later phase, but these are not event-rate estimates [N5-F3]. Therefore, a direct “median seizure events per patient year” comparison cannot be cleanly extracted from the provided evidence; the strongest available comparisons are in terms of responder rates, seizure freedom, and reduction in seizure frequency [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F3].

#### Which AEDs are most comparable to levetiracetam and under what conditions
The most directly comparable comparisons are with **lamotrigine** and **valproate**, because these are both used as first-line or adjunctive AEDs and appear in the same network meta-analysis and trial evidence [N1-F1][N4-R1][N5-F3]. Lamotrigine is especially relevant because the network meta-analysis found that lamotrigine and levetiracetam were more efficacious than other ASMs in children with drug-resistant focal-onset seizures, with levetiracetam having the highest probability of rank first for seizure freedom [N5-F3]. Valproate is also directly comparable because it is frequently used in generalized-onset or difficult-to-classify seizures and showed better seizure-free rates than topiramate in one trial [N4-R5]. However, valproate is less directly comparable to levetiracetam in focal-onset or partial-onset settings, where levetiracetam may be more favorable in monotherapy and adjunctive use [N1-F1][N1-F2].

The best direct comparisons are therefore:
- **Lamotrigine** in children with drug-resistant focal-onset seizures [N5-F3]
- **Valproate** in generalized-onset or difficult-to-classify seizures [N4-R5]
- **Valproate** versus other AEDs in observational comparisons [N4-R4]

### 2) Subgroup differences in seizure outcomes

#### How seizure rates vary by age, seizure type, epilepsy syndrome, and comorbidities
The evidence shows that seizure outcomes are not uniform across patient groups. In the Glasgow levetiracetam monotherapy study, seizure freedom was highest in **idiopathic generalized epilepsies** (54.2%) and **unclassified GTCS** (62.5%), and somewhat lower in **partial-onset seizures** (46.6%) [N1-F2]. This suggests that generalized or atypical generalized seizure types may respond better to levetiracetam than focal-onset seizures, at least in this monotherapy setting [N1-F2]. The same study also found that patients with **<5 seizures before starting levetiracetam** were more likely to become seizure-free than those with **≥5 seizures**, indicating that pretreatment seizure burden affects response [N1-F2].

Age-related differences are also present. The evidence notes that older adults generally respond better to ASMs and often require lower doses of ASM monotherapy, although this is more indirect evidence [N8-R3]. A comparative study in older adults reported lamotrigine had the highest 12-month seizure-freedom rate (54%), followed by levetiracetam (43%), when stratified into nonrefractory and refractory groups [N8-R4]. This suggests that levetiracetam may still be a reasonable option in older adults, but its efficacy may be somewhat lower than lamotrigine in some older adult cohorts [N8-R4]. Overall, seizure outcomes appear to vary by age, with older adults possibly responding differently than younger patients, though the evidence is more indirect for older adults than for children [N8-R3][N8-R4].

#### How treatment history and prior AED exposure affect outcomes
Treatment history and prior AED exposure strongly influence outcomes. In the Glasgow study, seizure freedom was higher when levetiracetam was used as **first monotherapy** (54.4%) than when patients were **switched from another AED** (39.2%) [N1-F2]. Patients who switched after failing a first or second AED had better outcomes than those who switched later in treatment, indicating that prior AED exposure and treatment failure history affect response [N1-F2]. The network meta-analysis also emphasizes that ASM selection should consider treatment history, comorbidities, side effects, and other patient factors [N5-F3]. The broader epilepsy literature adds that psychiatric comorbidities are linked to worse outcomes and may predict non-adherence and worse seizure control [N10-R2]. In the provided evidence, adherence is also implied as a factor: ASM adherence was reported to reach 40% and is regarded as a cause of breakthrough seizures [N10-R4]. These findings suggest that prior AED exposure, treatment failure, and adherence are important determinants of outcome.

The evidence indicates that treatment effects can vary substantially across subgroups. In the Glasgow study, the largest treatment effect was seen in patients with **fewer pretreatment seizures** and in **idiopathic generalized epilepsies**, where seizure freedom was highest [N1-F2]. In contrast, patients with more frequent pretreatment seizures or those switching from another AED had smaller treatment effects [N1-F2]. The network meta-analysis also suggests that levetiracetam and lamotrigine are among the most efficacious ASMs in children with drug-resistant focal-onset seizures, but it does not provide precise subgroup-specific rate differences [N5-F3]. Overall, the subgroup with the largest treatment effect is likely patients with fewer pretreatment seizures and those in idiopathic generalized syndromes, while patients with frequent pretreatment seizures, older adults, and those switching from another AED may show smaller treatment effects [N1-F2][N8-R4].

The evidence also suggests that treatment effects are not uniform across seizure types and epilepsy syndromes. Levetiracetam monotherapy showed good outcomes in **partial-onset seizures**, **idiopathic generalized epilepsies**, and **unclassified GTCS**, but the exact degree of benefit varied by syndrome [N1-F2]. The evidence also notes that levetiracetam is effective as adjunctive therapy for **refractory partial-onset seizures**, **primary generalized tonic-clonic seizures**, and **myoclonic seizures of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy**, and that it was equivalent to controlled release carbamazepine in partial-onset seizures [N1-F1]. These findings support the idea that treatment effects are largest in syndromes where levetiracetam’s mechanism and labeling are most aligned, such as generalized-onset or myoclonic seizures [N1-F1][N1-F2]. In contrast, the evidence does not strongly support a similar broad superiority for levetiracetam in all subgroups, and subgroup effects are therefore important [N1-F1][N1-F2].

#### Strength of evidence for each comparison and subgroup
The evidence is strongest for direct comparisons in specific subgroups. The Glasgow levetiracetam monotherapy study is a well-characterized real-world audit with detailed subgroup analysis by seizure type and syndrome, making it a strong source for subgroup conclusions [N1-F2]. However, it is an indirect comparison and should not be interpreted as a direct rate estimate for all AEDs [N5-F3]. Trial evidence is also strong for head-to-head comparisons, but the comparator evidence provided here is less precise for exact seizure rates than for responder rates or seizure freedom [N1-F1][N4-R1]. The main limitations are heterogeneity, nonrandomized design, and imprecision in outcome reporting. Network meta-analyses are limited by nonsystematic selection of RCTs, unexplored heterogeneity between studies, and selection of AEDs and dosing strategies that may not reflect clinical practice [N6-F4]. Observational RWE studies are limited by sample size, design, and lack of adjustment for baseline differences, so they are not robust for comparative conclusions [N6-F4]. The Glasgow study, while real-world and detailed, still depends on clinical recordkeeping and may miss subtle differences in seizure frequency or event timing [N1-F2]. The search results also note that variability in seizure rates across individuals contributes to uncertainty in treatment comparisons [N6-R2]. These limitations mean that conclusions should be cautious and interpreted as relative rather than absolute.
